title: Section 199A QBI deduction optimization
summary: A 20% deduction on qualified business income, with income-based phase-outs and SSTB exclusions.
detailsHtml:
How it works

The Qualified Business Income deduction allows pass-through business owners (sole props, LLCs, S-corps, partnerships) to deduct 20% of qualified business income from their personal income, reducing federal income tax. For a contractor in the 24% bracket, this is effectively a 4.8 percentage point cut on business income.

The SSTB problem

"Specified Service Trades or Businesses" (SSTBs) — including health, law, accounting, consulting, performing arts, financial services, and "any trade or business where the principal asset is the reputation or skill of one or more employees" — face full phase-out of the QBI deduction above income thresholds. For 2026, the phase-out begins at $201,775 single / $403,550 MFJ and completes at $276,775 single / $553,550 MFJ (Rev. Proc. 2025-32) — OBBBA expanded the phase-in window from $50K/$100K to $75K/$150K, materially widening the partial-deduction zone. Above the upper end, SSTBs get nothing. Non-SSTB businesses face W-2-wage and unadjusted-basis limitations but can retain partial deductions. Engineering and architecture are specifically excluded from SSTB classification — they qualify for the full deduction regardless of income. The threshold is measured against taxable income computed before the QBI deduction itself (IRC §199A(e)(2)) — not AGI, not gross income, not net business income alone. This catches taxpayers and preparers routinely: a household at $390K AGI may sit above or below the MFJ threshold depending on standard-vs-itemized choices, retirement contributions, HSA contributions, and capital-loss carryovers that move taxable income but not AGI.

This creates a hard income cliff for many consultants. Earning the dollar that pushes you over the SSTB threshold can cost you more in lost QBI deduction than the dollar itself was worth. Strategies include retirement contributions (which reduce QBI income), pre-tax HSA contributions, and timing income across years.
OBBBA $400 minimum (new for 2026): If your QBI is at least $1,000 and you materially participate in the business, you're guaranteed at least a $400 deduction even if standard calculations or SSTB phase-outs would produce less. Doesn't help SSTB owners fully phased out, but useful for small or marginal businesses.

Non-SSTB W-2 wage + UBIA limitation above threshold

For non-SSTB businesses above the threshold, the deduction is not capped at the SSTB-style phase-out — instead §199A(b)(2) imposes a different limit: the QBI deduction is the lesser of (a) 20% of QBI, or (b) the greater of 50% of W-2 wages paid by the business, or 25% of W-2 wages + 2.5% of the unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition (UBIA) of qualified depreciable property. Treas. Reg. §1.199A-1(d) provides the mechanics. This is the operative lever for capital-intensive non-SSTB businesses (real estate operating companies, manufacturing with substantial PP&E, equipment-rental businesses): the 25%-of-wages + 2.5%-of-UBIA prong rewards UBIA-heavy structures and frequently dominates the 50%-of-wages prong. The planning levers above the threshold are not AGI reduction (which is the SSTB lever) but rather W-2 wage restructuring (raising owner W-2 wage in S-corps, which has SE-tax tradeoffs; adding employees) and capital-asset acquisitions (which expand UBIA). Engineering and architecture, despite being service businesses, are statutorily excluded from SSTB and benefit from this same non-SSTB calculation. An experienced small-business CPA models the lesser-of analysis annually for any non-SSTB owner crossing the threshold.
